syllabus.quote: Explain set out purposes or reasons/make the relationships between things clear/say why and/or how and support with relevant evidence

one_line: Make a point, then give its reason with a linking word such as 'because' or 'so'. Do this for each mark you need.

points.heading: Statement, then reason
points.text: An explanation has two parts. First you make a statement, then you add a reason, a purpose or more detail about that statement.

cites.quote: An explanation requires a statement or description followed by a reason or purpose or further expansion of that statement

points.heading: Statement, then reason
points.text: Join the statement to its reason with a linking word such as 'so', 'so that', 'because' or 'which means'. The mark schemes and examiner reports put these words where the reason starts. Write the linking word in your answer too.

cites.quote: The lower the sample rate, the smaller the file size (1st) – because there is less data stored (1)

points.heading: First marks and follow-on marks
points.text: Some Explain mark schemes label a statement (1st) and the reason or detail under it (1). The (1) mark is only for the reason or detail you add to that statement. The (1st) label works as in the general rules at the front. 176 Explain parts appeared from 2022 to March 2026, and 174 have a mark scheme. 38 of those 174 mark schemes use (1st).

cites.quote: The sampling rate can affect the quality of audio files/how the audio sounds (1st) – because it captures sounds at discrete points (and not the whole sound) (1)

points.heading: First marks and follow-on marks
points.text: A statement with no reason can still get its one mark, and no more. If every point you write is only a statement, the mark scheme can stop you getting full marks.

cites.quote: A less detailed answer, such as 'they can learn at their own pace' can be given credit as it is a correct statement of the effect, but it lacks the detail to gain any further credit because it does not add an expansion
MAX two marks if answers are all only first marks.

points.heading: First marks and follow-on marks
points.text: Sometimes the mark scheme links a reason or detail to a first point. The reason then earns its mark only if you also make that first point. In one encryption question, the two further marks went only to answers that first said encryption scrambles the data. In a 2-mark question, one full point and its reason can be the whole answer.

cites.quote: A relatively easy first mark was given for any answer that stated that the data is scrambled. Many candidates achieved this mark. Two further marks were then dependant on this answer.
Max two for one complete explanation

points.heading: Reasons that fit the question
points.text: Explain asks why or how. Examiner reports say that many answers described what something is and lost marks.

cites.quote: there is usually little or no credit given for describing what the point or process is since this does not answer the question 'how'

points.heading: Reasons that fit the question
points.text: A common mistake is to leave out the reason. A short phrase such as 'makes the code more readable' does not get full marks.

cites.quote: A common mistake was to omit a reason or expansion to the response – the question asked for explanations
a significant number only stated that comment make the code more readable so did not gain the full marks.

points.heading: Reasons that fit the question
points.text: Use exact technical words. In one encryption question, many answers said encrypted data 'cannot be understood', and a similar number said it 'cannot be read'. Only 'cannot be understood' got the mark.

cites.quote: Many candidates made the point that encrypted data can not be understood, but an approximately equal number stated that encrypted data could not be read, and were not awarded marks.

points.heading: Reasons that fit the question
points.text: If the question has a scenario, use it. Give reasons that fit the situation in the question. A general fact that ignores the scenario cannot reach the full range of marks.

cites.quote: The full range of marks is only available to candidates for answers referring to the scenario in the questions.

question.quote: Mainframe computers were developed from the need for computers to process data in tasks such as carrying out a census. (c) Explain why mainframe computers are used to process the data from a census.

strong.sentence: A census collects a very large amount of data that the computer has to process,

earns.quote: The amount of data that has to be processed is very large (1st)

strong.sentence: as countries tend to have a lot of people and each person adds more data.

earns.quote: as countries tend to have a lot of people (1)

strong.sentence: The computer also needs to process all of this data in a short time, so a mainframe with a high processing speed does the work.

earns.quote: All data needs to be processed in a short period of time (1st)

weak.answer: There is a lot of data in a census. Mainframes are very reliable.
weak.why: Both sentences are only first marks, with no reason after them. The mark scheme gives a maximum of 2 marks when all the answers are only first marks. The examiners also said that most answers stopped at 'a large amount of data'.

basis.quote: Typically, however, responses tended to focus on that fact that there is usually a large amount of data.

question.quote: Explain how each of these methods keeps data safe from unauthorised users. (a) encryption

strong.sentence: so that anyone who intercepts it cannot understand it,
which means the data is of no use to a hacker or any other third party.

earns.quote: of no use to a hacker/third party (1)

weak.answer: Encryption makes the data unreadable so hackers cannot read it.
weak.why: It never says that encryption scrambles the data. That first mark is missing, and the two marks that depend on it go with it. The examiners wanted 'cannot be understood', and 'cannot be read' is the wrong idea.

basis.quote: Rather than making data unreadable, encryption puts data into a state whereby it can not be understood.

thin_evidence: 176 parts, and 174 of them have a mark scheme. 38 of those 174 mark schemes use the (1st) and (1) labels. The rest give one mark for each point. Only one mark scheme, for Q3(c) on Paper 13 in November 2023, limits answers that are 'all only first marks'.
